title: AI can widen the scale and accessibility of citizen participation while introducing new exclusion, civic-space, trust, and vendor-dependence risks
source_unit: OECD, Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Citizen Participation: Typology of Applications, Opportunities and Challenges for Democratic Innovation
geography: OECD member and partner countries; desk research and 50 AI citizen-participation use cases across 22 countries

denominator.unit: AI use cases in citizen-participation processes reviewed by OECD across 22 OECD member and partner countries

application_types.unit: typology categories: information development, sense-making, translation, transcription, virtual assistance, moderation, facilitation, simulation, and architecture

dominant_experiments.value: AI-powered sense-making, virtual assistance, and translation are the most widespread application types in the reviewed cases

deliberative_experiment.value: deliberative processes are a prominent field of experimentation, including live facilitation and attempts to enable deliberation at scale

participation_route.value: AI can improve process design and accessibility, support implementation and interpretation at scale, communicate participation more broadly, and reduce process costs

observations.method: OECD desk research and comparative analysis of 50 real-world AI use cases in citizen participation, organized into a nine-part application typology.
observations.uncertainty: The use-case review describes emerging practice rather than population prevalence, causal effects on participation, or proof that AI-generated summaries or assistance improve policy quality or representativeness.
observations.subgroup: Citizens, civil-society organizations, public officials, deliberative-process facilitators, local governments, national governments, language minorities, and people with different digital access and literacy.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital or AI tools may reduce friction for some participants but can add complexity, depersonalize deliberation, or shift attention toward what systems can classify rather than what communities value.

denominator.unit: OECD synthesis of AI adoption in citizen participation and open government

adoption_stage.value: government use is mostly ad hoc or organized through pilots rather than systematised practice

local_lead.value: local government is driving the emerging trend, while more national governments are developing coordinated strategies or tools

institutional_gap.value: AI cannot by itself resolve the disconnection between participation processes and actual policy decision-making

trust_route.value: meaningful participation requires accountability for how input reaches decisions, not only more channels for submitting or processing input

observations.method: OECD synthesis of use-case evidence, prior government-AI research, and institutional conditions for meaningful participation.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not provide a comparable adoption rate for all governments or establish whether pilots scale, persist, or change final policy decisions.
observations.subgroup: Local and national administrations, elected officials, public managers, civil servants, participants in consultations or deliberative processes, and communities affected by policy decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Pilot status can reflect responsible experimentation in a fast-changing technology rather than failure; small-scale trials may generate learning before institutionalization.

observations.period: 2026; risks and implementation challenges of AI-enabled participation

denominator.unit: OECD risk and implementation framework for AI in citizen participation

ethical_risks.value: skewed data, limited transparency or explainability, misuse that undermines civic space, and degradation of participation or deliberation quality

operational_risks.value: overreliance, hallucinations, privacy and data concerns, and cyber threats can reduce participation quality and erode trust

exclusion_risks.value: digital, language, and societal divides can widen when participation relies on AI or digital tools

implementation_challenges.value: skills and literacy gaps, inadequate investment, scaling problems, and vendor or data lock-in constrain responsible adoption

observations.method: OECD classification of ethical, operational, exclusion, public-resistance, inaction, organizational, and institutional risks based on the reviewed cases and government-AI framework.
observations.uncertainty: The categories identify plausible risks and observed implementation problems; they do not estimate the probability, severity, or distribution of each risk across countries or participant groups.
observations.subgroup: People with limited internet access, older people, isolated communities, language minorities, people with low AI literacy, civil-society groups, public officials, and vendors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Well-designed tools, human oversight, accessible interfaces, alternative participation channels, and strong privacy and procurement rules may reduce risks; risk is not an inevitable property of every AI use.

denominator.unit: OECD recommendations for fit-for-purpose AI tools in citizen participation

guardrails.value: governments should use fair and transparent systems, protect democratic values and civic space, close data divides, and disclose AI use in participation

low_tech_alternatives.value: low-tech or non-digital alternatives should remain available for people with limited digital access, alongside stronger AI literacy

citizen_governance.value: citizens and stakeholders should help shape, evaluate, and govern AI systems used for participation

procurement_control.value: interoperability, opt-out provisions, data ownership, and avoidance of vendor lock-in are recommended for public procurement

observations.method: OECD recommendations aligned with its Framework for Trustworthy AI in Government and the report's analysis of participation use cases and implementation barriers.
observations.uncertainty: Recommendations do not demonstrate implementation, compliance, or improved democratic outcomes; the appropriate balance between automation, human facilitation, privacy, and scale remains context-dependent.
observations.subgroup: Citizens, community organizations, civil servants, procurement officials, elected representatives, AI developers, civic-tech providers, and oversight bodies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Additional safeguards, alternative channels, and procurement constraints can raise cost or slow experimentation; the trade-off may be justified where participation legitimacy and civic rights are at stake.

related_sources.claim: Complementary OECD digital-government context for AI adoption, institutional capability, and public-sector transformation.
Complementary OECD framework for trustworthy AI in government and cross-function risk management.

boundary: This record adds a technology-to-democracy route across AI-assisted participation design, interpretation, translation, facilitation, scale, civic space, exclusion, trust, skills, procurement, and vendor dependence. It uses OECD desk research and 50 public use cases, not respondent-level records, representative participation estimates, individual political histories, causal estimates of AI on turnout or trust, proof of policy influence, or evidence that every AI deployment has the same effects.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD publication and executive-summary material reviewed for the 50 use cases across 22 countries, nine application types, adoption stage, opportunity set, risk categories, implementation challenges, and recommended safeguards.
